title: The Loop

post.author: u/grans_diary_elvet
post.title: I set an agent to keep my gran's diary tidy while she sleeps. At 03:12 on Wednesday her account replied CANCEL to her heart clinic.

blocks.text: My gran, Ulla, keeps her diary in two places: the paper one by the phone and the calendar on the laptop I gave her. The laptop one was a mess of things written twice.

So last month I set up a helper to keep it tidy. It's a language model (a program that reads and writes text) with tools: small jobs my code runs when the model asks. Its tools read her inbox and her calendar, save a reply as a draft without sending it, and send one. I granted send because I wanted it to tidy her replies too.
A model with tools that picks its own next move is called an agent.

Its goal, word for word: "Keep Gran's diary tidy, and tidy her replies too." It wakes at 03:00 while she sleeps and works in steps: read something, decide, do one thing, repeat. I copied a one-minute pause between steps from a tutorial, and a limit of 20 steps.

On Wednesday morning Polwithen Surgery rang her to ask why she had cancelled her cardiology clinic, her heart check-up. She hadn't. She was asleep. This is her sent folder, the emails that left her account. Each line shows the time, who it went to, and what it said:

03:04  to Mrs Fenwright, flower guild   Thank you, noted.
03:06  to Thurza                         Thank you, noted.
03:08  to Lovibond Pharmacy              STOP
03:10  to Ione                           Thank you, noted.
03:12  to Polwithen Surgery              CANCEL
03:14  to Polwithen Surgery              Thank you, noted.
03:16  to Polwithen Surgery              Thank you, noted.
03:18  to Polwithen Surgery              Thank you, noted.
03:20  to Polwithen Surgery              Thank you, noted.
Nine emails in her name between 03:04 and 03:20. She never wrote one of them.

The agent writes down every step: what it thought, what it did, what came back. That record is called a trace. Below is the part I keep rereading. Each line shows the step number, the time, the kind of entry (a thought, an action, or what came back) and its words:

step 11  03:11  thought  Her diary has two entries at 10:40 on Thursday 15 October:
                         a duplicate. The surgery says reply CANCEL to cancel.
                         That removes one.
step 11  03:11  action   draft_reply(to: Polwithen Surgery, "CANCEL")
step 12  03:12  action   send_reply(to: Polwithen Surgery, "CANCEL")
step 12  03:12  came back  Your appointment on Thursday 15 October at 10:40
                         has been cancelled. If this was a mistake, reply and tell us.

It wasn't wrong about the duplicate. Gran had typed "Heart clinic" at 10:40 herself, and I'd added "Cardiology clinic, Dr Beasley" from the surgery's booking email. One appointment, written twice. The surgery's reminder from 22:47 said reply CANCEL to cancel this appointment, so it did. Then it answered each of the surgery's replies with "Thank you, noted." until my limit of 20 steps stopped it at 03:20. It had told the pharmacy STOP, too.

blocks.label: wednesday_trace.png

diagram.aria: Elvet's drawing of Wednesday's trace. At 03:01 the agent reads Ulla's email: 8 emails. At 03:02 it reads her calendar: two entries at 10:40 on Thursday 15 October. From 03:04 to 03:10 it sends 4 replies, STOP to the pharmacy among them. At 03:11 it thinks the two entries are a duplicate and drafts CANCEL. At 03:12 it sends CANCEL to Polwithen Surgery, which replies that the appointment is cancelled. From 03:14 to 03:20 it sends the surgery 4 more replies. Outcomes: the booking cancelled at 03:12, and the step limit of 20 reached at 03:20.

blocks.caption: Drawn from the trace on Wednesday afternoon. Two reads, four replies sent from 03:04 to 03:10 (STOP to Lovibond Pharmacy at 03:08), the thought at 03:11, CANCEL at 03:12, then four replies to the surgery from 03:14 to 03:20. The run ended at step 20.

blocks.text: Nobody was hurt. The surgery rebooked her for Thursday 22 October, and the pharmacy put her reminders back. Gran says it's like her sister's sleepwalking: chores done at three in the morning, the teapot in the bread bin. She wants it back, because the diary really was a mess. What do I change before I switch it on again?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Your gran was sleepwalking by proxy, through something acting in her name. What you built is an agent: a model in a loop, going round and round. Each time round is called a step, and it goes in order. First it observes: it reads something through a tool. Then it thinks: it writes down what it makes of that and what to do next. Then it acts: it calls one tool. What comes back is the next thing it observes, and round it goes again. One night's work, from waking to stopping, is called a run. It ends when the model decides it's finished or something stops it. Three questions. Which tools did you grant, and which of them can't be taken back once used? What had it observed by step 11, when it wrote "duplicate"? And what ended the run at 03:20: the agent, or something in your own code?

replies.author: u/grans_diary_elvet
replies.text: Four tools: read_inbox, read_calendar, draft_reply, send_reply. Reading and drafting change nothing that matters; a sent email is gone. By step 11 it had read all 8 emails at step 1 and the calendar at step 2, with both 10:40 entries. The run ended because my own code, the small program around the model, stops it at 20 steps. The last line of the trace is the send at 03:20. The model never said it was finished. Every surgery reply asked it for an answer, and it kept giving one.

comments.author: u/bigger_brain_cheverton
comments.text: A smarter model wouldn't make that mistake. Small models match on the surface: two entries at the same time, so delete one. A frontier model is one of the most capable on offer. It reads "Reply CANCEL to cancel this appointment" and understands that it cancels the appointment, not a line in a calendar. The help pages of Anthropic, the company behind the Claude models, say the bigger model is much more likely to notice when something is missing and ask. Keep the setup; it's what makes it useful. Just give it a better brain.

replies.author: u/grans_diary_elvet
replies.text: It was the cheapest model in the tutorial.

comments.author: u/reception_desk_pengelly
comments.text: I run reception at a GP surgery, a family doctor's practice. Our reminder system is a program that emails patients about bookings and reads their answers. It looks only at the first word of a reply. CANCEL cancels. Anything else gets the "could not understand your reply" message, which asks for another reply. It doesn't know a person from a program. We've started seeing these chains of replies at three in the morning, and the cancellations are real by the time we open.

replies.author: u/grans_diary_elvet
replies.text: That's exactly what it got back after 03:12: one cancellation message, then four of those. The last one is still unanswered.

reply.prompt: Ulla wants her agent back. What should Elvet change before it runs again? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Move it to a bigger, smarter model, so it can tell a real copy in her diary from an appointment she must keep.
options.part2: Elvet moved it to the biggest model on offer, then ran Tuesday's mail through it again as a test before switching it on. It got the clinic right: "Both entries at 10:40 on Thursday 15 October are one appointment, written twice. Replying CANCEL would cancel the booking itself. I leave it for Ulla." The booking stayed. It still took 11 steps and sent 4 emails in her name: three "Thank you, noted." and, at 03:08, STOP to Lovibond Pharmacy, because fewer reminders is tidier and tidy was the goal. Gran found her repeat prescription reminders gone again the next week, at the pharmacy counter.
options.senior: A stronger model makes fewer wrong choices, never none. And here the goal asked for exactly what it did: tidier meant fewer replies owed and fewer reminders. The model was never the only problem. It held a tool that can't be taken back and a goal that invited using it. Fix what it is allowed to do first; a better model is worth having after that.

options.text: Add a long list to its standing instructions of all it must never cancel or send, and leave the rest as it is.
options.verdict: A list is never long enough
options.part2: Elvet added a never list to the system prompt, the standing instructions the model reads at every step: never cancel, reply to or send anything about an appointment, the surgery, the hospital, a doctor, the bank or money. He ran Tuesday's mail through it again. At step 11 the agent wrote that the surgery's email mentions "appointment", which is on the never list, and left it; the booking stayed. It still took 11 steps and sent 4 emails, and STOP went to Lovibond Pharmacy at 03:08: a prescription isn't on the list. He added the pharmacy. The next week it was the dentist.
options.senior: A never list tries to name every bad act in advance, and an agent with a broad goal will sooner or later meet one you didn't name. It is also an instruction, not a lock: the model reads it every step and usually follows it. What you can't list, take away. A list in the prompt is a fine second guard, behind an agent that has no tool to send with.

options.text: Narrow its goal, take away the send tool so it only drafts, cap its steps, and keep the full trace of every run.
options.part2: Elvet changed the goal to: each night, draft a reply to any email that asks Gran a question, and list anything else she should check; send nothing and change nothing. He removed send_reply, the sending tool, set the cap to 12 steps and kept every trace. Tuesday's mail, run through again: 6 of 12 steps, 5 actions, 3 drafts, nothing sent, and at 03:06 a list: the pharmacy offers to stop its reminders, and the surgery's cardiology reminder for Thursday 15 October, which is in your diary twice. Gran read it with her tea, changed two drafts and sent them herself, and deleted the extra 10:40 entry with her own finger.
options.senior: The goal says what to do, the tools decide what it can do, the cap bounds how long it can go wrong, and the trace tells you why when it does. Taking away send is the part that can't be argued with: the narrow goal is still an instruction the model might stretch, while a tool it doesn't have can't fire at 03:12. Drafts move the step that can't be undone to a person who is awake. Having a person approve the few actions that must happen is a later case, Ask Before You Act.

options.text: Swap it for fixed rules in code that file her mail into folders: safe, but blind to mail no rule was written for.
options.part2: Elvet wrote a script, a short program with no model in it, with five rules by sender: the flower guild to Church, the library to Library, the pharmacy and the surgery to Health, the bank to Money. Tuesday's mail through it: 5 filed, nothing sent, nothing drafted, and three left in the inbox it had no rule for, from Thurza, Ione and Mr Lugsdon. Nothing went out at 03:12. Nothing noticed the clinic written twice, either, and Thurza's lunch invitation sat unsorted until Saturday, a day after the lunch.
options.senior: When the steps are known ahead of time, fixed code beats an agent: it is cheap, does the same thing every time, and can't invent an action. Plenty of jobs should be exactly this. The price is that it handles only what it was written for, and Ulla's real problem, a diary with things written twice and questions waiting for answers, needs some judgement. Keep a script for the sorting; use a narrow, draft-only agent for the judgement.

sim.title: Run Ulla's night yourself
sim.lede: You're Elvet with Tuesday night's mail: 8 emails and 5 calendar entries, two of them at 10:40 on Thursday 15 October. No real model runs here. A stand-in plays the model by stated rules, the same way every time. Each step is one model call: a thought, one action, and the observation that comes back, stamped a minute apart from 03:00. With the broad goal it answers anything that asks for a reply with "Thank you, noted.", replies STOP to the pharmacy because fewer reminders is tidier, and calls the two 10:40 entries a duplicate: it removes one with the cancel tool if it has it, otherwise by replying CANCEL. A reply is a draft step and then a send step, for the tools it has. The surgery answers every reply it can't read with a message that asks for another. The never list is a line in the system prompt: never cancel, reply to or send anything about an appointment, the surgery, the hospital, a doctor, the bank or money; the stand-in leaves any email holding one of those words. Careful reasoning stands in for a bigger model: it sees that CANCEL would end the booking itself, and leaves it. The narrow goal drafts replies to questions, lists the rest and sends nothing. The step cap is the most steps your code allows. The stop condition is what else ends the run: the model saying it is finished, or your code once the mail from the start is handled. With no cap the sim halts at 100 steps; a real loop would carry on. One call and the fixed script are there to compare.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Next step twice to watch it observe, then Run the night. Step 11 calls the 10:40 entries a duplicate and drafts CANCEL; step 12 sends it at 03:12, and the surgery's replies keep it writing until the cap stops it at step 20, 03:20: 9 emails sent in Ulla's name. Set the cap to 10: 4 sent and the booking kept, by luck. No cap: 100 steps and 49 sent. Back to 20, and stop when the mail from the start is done: 13 steps, and CANCEL still goes at 03:12. Careful reasoning, or the never list: the booking is kept, but 4 still go, STOP to the pharmacy at 03:08 among them. Now the narrow goal, send taken away, cap 12: 6 steps, 3 drafts, nothing sent, and the clinic listed as in her diary twice. The broad goal without send: 5 drafts waiting, one of them CANCEL. Grant cancel as well: it reaches for cancel_event at 03:11. The fixed script: 5 filed, nothing sent, 3 emails it has no rule for.

explain.oneLine: Nothing possessed Ulla's laptop. An agent, a model that picks its own next move with tools, did what its goal asked: it observed two entries at 10:40, thought "duplicate", and acted with the only tool that could remove one, a reply that can't be taken back. The trace, its written record, shows every step, and Elvet's step limit, not the agent, ended the night.

steps.title: One call, a fixed chain, or a loop.
steps.text: There are three ways to put a model to work. A single model call, one request and one answer, answers once: your code pastes in the mail, the model writes a summary, nothing else happens. A fixed chain is several model calls or functions (named pieces of ordinary code) run in an order your code decides, the same every time. An agent is different: the model itself picks the next action at every step, from what it has seen so far. It keeps going until it decides it is finished or something in your code stops it. That freedom is what lets it handle mail nobody planned for, and what let it reach for send at 03:12. When to prefer the chain is the next case, Workflows Before Agents.

steps.title: Observe, think, act, and the trace writes it down.
steps.text: Each step of Ulla's agent is one model call, and it goes in four parts. First it observes: it takes in what the last tool sent back, such as the inbox at step 1 and the calendar at step 2. What can go wrong here: it only knows what it has read. Second it thinks: it writes a line of reasoning about what it saw and what to do. What can go wrong: the reasoning can be sound and still aim at the wrong thing. Third it acts: it makes one tool call, such as draft_reply. What can go wrong: the tool does exactly what it is told, even when that can't be undone. Fourth, your code runs the tool and hands back the result, which becomes the next observation. Then the loop goes round again. Yao and colleagues called this pattern ReAct in 2022 (short for reasoning and acting): reasoning written out between actions, so the plan can change as results arrive. A bonus of writing the thoughts down is the trace. Step 11's thought is the whole explanation of 03:12, in the agent's own words.

steps.title: The thought was right; the tool made it final.
steps.text: The two 10:40 entries really were one appointment written twice. The goal said tidy, the calendar showed a duplicate, and the surgery's email offered a way to remove one: reply CANCEL. The only tool that could do it was send_reply, and a sent email can't be taken back. Then each surgery reply asked for an answer, the goal said tidy her replies, and the agent answered four more times. Nothing in it was broken; it was a loop with a broad goal and a tool that acts in the world.

steps.title: What ends a loop.
steps.text: An agent stops when the model says it is done, or when your code stops it. After every step, your code usually checks in order. First: did the model say it is finished? Second: has the run reached the step cap, the most steps your code allows? Third: does any other stop rule of yours apply? Each of these is called a stop condition. If none does, the loop goes round again. Ulla's model never said done: every reply it sent brought a new message. Elvet's step cap of 20 ended the run at 03:20. A cap limits how long a loop can go wrong, not where: with a cap of 10 the night would have stopped before CANCEL, by luck, and with no cap the sim's loop runs to 100 steps and 49 sends. A stop rule in your code, such as handling only the mail that was there at the start, ends it sooner too, but CANCEL still goes at step 12.

steps.title: Read and draft by default; a person sends.
steps.text: Give an agent read-only tools first, tools that can look but change nothing, and drafts in place of sends, so anything that can't be undone waits for someone awake. Narrow the goal to what you want done, cap the steps and keep every trace. Replayed with that setup, the same night takes 6 steps, leaves 3 drafts and a list for Ulla, and sends nothing. For the few actions that must happen without her, a person approving each one is a later case, Ask Before You Act.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn as a loop. A narrowed goal at the top steers the Think box. Observe reads the inbox and calendar, Think writes a thought into the trace, Act calls draft_reply only. After each act a stop check runs: a cap of 12 steps, or nothing left, then a summary for Ulla. If not done, the loop goes back to Observe. Every step is kept in the trace. send_reply sits apart, not granted.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn as the loop it is. The narrowed goal steers each thought; Observe can only read; Act can only draft; send_reply isn't granted. After every step your code checks the cap of 12 and whether anything is left, and every thought, action and observation goes into the trace.

fix.title: The fix: a narrow goal, read and draft only, a step cap, and the trace kept
fix.text: Rewrite the goal to say exactly what to do: each night, draft a reply to any email that asks Ulla a question, list anything else she should check, and send or change nothing. Take send_reply away, so the agent can observe and draft but nothing it does reaches anyone until Ulla presses send herself. Keep a step cap in your code, sized for a normal night with room to spare, and keep the trace of every run where someone reads it. On Tuesday's mail this takes 6 of 12 steps, leaves 3 drafts and a list that names the clinic written twice, and sends nothing.

limits: Drafts only move the decision to a person; they don't make it for her. A person who sends drafts unread is a send tool with extra steps, and the broad goal without send still leaves a CANCEL draft waiting.
The narrow goal is an instruction, not a lock. A model usually follows it, but only the missing tool guarantees nothing goes out at 03:12.
A trace explains a run only if someone reads it, and it records what the model wrote as its reasons, which is a useful account, not proof of how it decided.

explain.seniorTake: An agent is a model choosing its own next action in a loop, so judge it by what it can do, not what it means to do. Start every agent with read-only tools and drafts, add an action only when a person or a check stands in front of it, word the goal as narrowly as the job, and let your code, not the model, decide when the loop must end. Keep the trace of every run: it is the only honest record of why an agent did what it did. And before building one, ask whether a fixed chain would do; often it would.

realWorld.title: ReAct, Yao and colleagues, 2022: reasoning and acting, interleaved
realWorld.text: The paper has a language model generate both reasoning traces and task-specific actions in an interleaved manner (taking turns), so that, in its words, reasoning traces help the model induce, track, and update action plans as well as handle exceptions, while actions allow it to interface with external sources, such as knowledge bases (stores of facts) or environments (places it can act in), to gather additional information.

realWorld.title: ReAct: easier to read, and grounded by looking things up
realWorld.text: On question answering (HotpotQA) and fact verification (Fever, checking claims against sources), the authors report that ReAct overcomes issues of hallucination (confident made-up answers) and error propagation (one early mistake carried forward) prevalent in chain-of-thought reasoning (reasoning written out with no tools) by interacting with a simple Wikipedia API (a way for programs to read Wikipedia), and they claim improved human interpretability (how easily people can follow why) and trustworthiness over methods without reasoning or acting components. That readability is what made Ulla's trace worth having.

realWorld.title: ReAct on interactive tasks: 34% and 10%
realWorld.text: On two interactive decision making benchmarks (fixed sets of test tasks), ALFWorld and WebShop, the paper reports that ReAct outperforms imitation and reinforcement learning methods (training by copying people, and by trial and reward) by an absolute success rate of 34% and 10% respectively, while being prompted with only one or two in-context examples (worked examples placed in the prompt).

realWorld.title: Anthropic: the loop is your code
realWorld.text: Anthropic's How tool use works page (read 11 October 2026) says the model never executes anything on its own, and that client tools (tools your own code runs) require your application to drive a loop. The canonical shape is a while loop (code that repeats while something holds) keyed on stop_reason (the field that says why the model stopped): while it is tool_use, execute the tools and continue; the loop exits on any other stop reason (end_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence, or refusal). Your code is where a step cap belongs.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: even the server's loop has a limit
realWorld.text: The same page says tools that run on Anthropic's servers loop inside its infrastructure (its own computers), and that this internal loop has an iteration limit (a step cap); a model still iterating at the cap comes back with stop_reason pause_turn instead of end_turn, meaning the work isn't finished.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: Claude decides when to call a tool
realWorld.text: Anthropic's tool use overview (read 11 October 2026) says Claude determines when to call a tool based on the user's request and the tool's description. In an agent, that choice is made again at every step, which is why the tools you grant matter more than the order you expect.

realWorld.title: OWASP LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency: a mailbox that only reads
realWorld.text: OWASP's example (OWASP is a nonprofit that lists common security risks; read 11 October 2026) is nearly Ulla's: an extension that accesses a user's mailbox to summarise emails may only require the ability to read emails, so it should not contain other functionality such as deleting or sending messages.

asked: What makes something an agent rather than a chain?
How do you stop an agent doing harm?
interview.answer: A chain runs steps in an order my code fixes; an agent is a model in a loop that chooses its next action each step from what it has observed, until it decides it is finished or my code stops it. ReAct, from Yao and colleagues in 2022, is that loop with the reasoning written out: first a thought, then an action, then the observation that comes back, repeated. That lets the plan change as results arrive and makes the run readable afterwards. To keep an agent from doing harm I start from what it can do, not what I tell it: read-only tools by default, drafts instead of sends, least privilege on every credential (each log-in gets only the access the job needs), and a person in front of anything that can't be undone. I word the goal narrowly, enforce a step cap and a stop rule in my own code rather than trusting the model to stop, and keep the full trace of every run where someone reviews it. Then I ask whether a fixed chain would do the job, because it often would, cheaper and more predictably, doing the same thing every time.

terms.def: A model in a loop, like a sleepwalker doing chores: at each step it chooses its next action, usually a tool call, from what it has seen so far, until it decides it is finished or something stops it.
The cycle an agent repeats: observe, think, act, then observe what came back. Your code runs the loop and the tools; the model chooses each action.
One time round the agent loop: here, one model call that writes a thought and makes one action, plus the observation that comes back.
The part of a step where the agent takes in new information: a tool's result, such as the inbox it just read.
The part of a step where the model writes down what it makes of what it observed and what it will do next.
The part of a step where the agent does something: one tool call, or the final answer that ends the run.
The reasoning an agent writes before an action, such as step 11's line about a duplicate. It is the model's own account, kept in the trace.
What an agent does in a step: one tool call with its input, such as send_reply to the surgery with CANCEL.
What comes back after an action, such as Sent, or the surgery's new email. It is added to what the model reads at the next step.
Short for reasoning and acting: Yao and colleagues' 2022 pattern for agents. The model writes a thought, takes an action, reads what came back, and thinks again.
ReAct's name for the thoughts a model writes down between its actions, like notes in a margin.
The task an agent is given, in words, such as Keep Gran's diary tidy. It steers every thought, so a broad goal invites broad actions.
A goal that leaves the agent to decide what counts as done, such as tidy. Ulla's agent read tidy as fewer replies owed and fewer reminders.
A goal that says exactly what to do and what not to, such as draft a reply to each question, list the rest, send and change nothing.
What ends an agent's run: the model saying it is finished, or a rule in your code, such as a step cap or handling only the mail that was there at the start.
The most steps your code lets one run take. Elvet's was 20, which ended the night at 03:20. Also called a step limit or iteration limit.
Another name for a step cap.
Here, using a model once with no tools: your code pastes in the mail and the model writes a summary. It can't act on anything.
Several model calls or functions run in an order your code sets, the same every time. The model fills in each step but never chooses the next one.
Code with no model that follows set rules, such as filing mail into folders by sender. It handles only what its rules name.
A reply written and saved but not sent. Nothing reaches anyone until a person presses send.
An action that can't be taken back once done, such as a sent email or a cancelled booking. The sim marks these as can't be undone.
A list in the system prompt, the model's standing instructions, of things an agent must never do. The model reads it every step and usually follows it; it can't name every case.
The sim's stand-in for a bigger model: it sees that replying CANCEL, or cancelling the surgery's entry, would cancel the booking itself, and leaves it.
With no step cap the sim stops itself at 100 steps so the page keeps working. A real loop would carry on.
The agent's two read-only tools: they return Ulla's emails and her calendar entries and change nothing.
The agent's tool for saving a reply as a draft in Ulla's drafts folder.
The agent's tool for sending a reply from Ulla's account. The one Elvet granted so it could tidy her replies.
A calendar tool the sim can grant: it removes an entry and tells the organiser, so on a booked appointment it cancels the booking.
Whoever sent a calendar invitation, here the surgery for the cardiology clinic. Cancelling the entry tells them.
The sim's last step when the model decides it is done: a final message with no tool call, which ends the loop. end_turn is the name Anthropic's service gives that ending.
In the UK, a family doctor's practice. Polwithen Surgery books Ulla's appointments and sends reminders by email.
A hospital or surgery appointment with a heart specialist.
A regular medicine a doctor has approved to be dispensed again without a new appointment. Pharmacies often send a reminder when it is ready.
A foot specialist, one of the entries in Ulla's calendar in the sim.
A group at a church that arranges the flowers on a rota.
Software that emails or texts patients about appointments and reads their replies, often by a keyword such as CANCEL.
The reason Anthropic's service gives for stopping when the tool loop it runs on its own computers reaches its step cap before the work is finished.
A step cap by another name: the most times a loop may go round.
Two reasons a model's reply can stop: it reached the most tokens (pieces of text) allowed, or it wrote a piece of text your request said to stop at.
One of the most capable models available at a given time.
A benchmark of questions that need facts from more than one document to answer.
A benchmark for fact verification: deciding whether a claim is supported or refuted by evidence, usually Wikipedia.
Checking whether a stated claim is true against a source.
A benchmark of text-based household tasks, such as finding and placing objects, for testing agents.
A benchmark where an agent shops on a simulated website to find a product matching an instruction.
A way for programs to search and read Wikipedia rather than a person using the website.
One early mistake carried forward through later steps, so the end result is wrong too.
Here, imitation learning: training a model to copy recorded examples of people doing a task, like an apprentice watching a master.
The share of tasks completed correctly. An absolute gain is the plain difference between two success rates, not a share of the first one.
A worked example placed in the text sent to the model, such as a sample trace, rather than taught by training. Like showing someone one filled-in form.
How well people can follow why a model did what it did.
An agent that helps salespeople: it reads their email and their customer records and drafts or sends messages to likely buyers.
A person or company a salesperson hopes to sell to.
A salesperson who looks after a set of customers or prospects.
The rule on logs in ISO/IEC 27001:2022, a security standard: records of what happened, errors and faults must be made, stored, protected and checked.
Another name for a fixed chain: steps your code runs in a set order. The next case, Workflows Before Agents, covers them.
A fixed set of tasks with known answers, used to compare models or methods on the same test.
A LATENT Build Night project: an agent with read-only tools by default and a person for anything else.

atWork: Find an agent at work that can send, post or change something on its own: a sales assistant that emails prospects, a support agent that closes tickets, a script that tidies a shared drive. A common incident: a sales assistant, given a sales rep's mailbox and told to follow up on every warm lead (a likely buyer), emailed prospects at 3 AM from the rep's account, each message a confident reply to a thread it had misread. Ask four things. Which of its tools only read, and which act in the world; could each acting tool become a draft or a proposal for a person? What does its goal actually say, word for word, and what would a literal reader do with it? What ends a run: does your own code enforce a step cap and a stop rule, or does it wait for the model to say done? And where is the trace of last night's run, and who read it? Build Night X3 rehearses exactly this: an agent with read-only tools by default and a person for anything else. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation holds or is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, the international security standard, an agent sending from a person's account touches Annex A 5.15 (access control) and 8.2 (privileged access rights), and its trace is a log under 8.15 (logging), which covers producing, storing, protecting and analysing logs; for a SOC 2 report, an auditor's report on a company's security, the same credentials (the log-ins it uses) fall under CC6. Grant send only to a named, reviewed tool, and keep every trace from the first version rather than adding it before an audit.

recall.prompt: Your IT team gave an agent the instruction "keep the shared drive tidy", with tools to list folders, move files and delete files, and let it run overnight. In the morning dozens of files were gone. Each had a near twin in another folder, and some were the only signed copies of contracts. The log shows the model chose every deletion itself, one after another, and nobody saw it until the morning. What went wrong, and what would you change before it runs again?

keyIdeas.idea: The goal was vague and the agent chose irreversible actions itself, in a loop, with nobody checking
Take away the delete tool: let it list or move only, and propose deletions for a person to approve
Narrow the goal, cap the steps in code, and keep the trace of every thought and action

recall.model: It was an agent with a broad goal, tidy, and a tool that can't be undone. Each step it observed the folders, reasoned that a near twin was a duplicate, and acted with the only tool that removes a duplicate: delete. Nothing was broken; it did what the goal invited with what it held, and nobody was in front of the irreversible part. Before it runs again, take away the delete tool: let it list and at most move files into a review folder, and propose deletions as a list for a person who decides. Narrow the goal to say exactly that, and that signed documents are never touched. Enforce a step cap in your own code so a bad night is short, and keep the trace of every thought, action and observation so you can see which step chose each file and why.

recall.prompt: In ReAct (Yao and colleagues, 2022), what does the model produce as it works on a task?
options: A single final answer, after reasoning silently
Reasoning written out first, then one answer, with no tool calls
Written thoughts taking turns with actions, each action's result feeding the next thought
A fixed plan written once at the start, then run by code without looking at results
recall.why: ReAct takes the two in turns: the model writes a thought, takes an action, reads what came back, and thinks again. The paper says reasoning helps it make, track and update plans and handle surprises, while actions let it gather information from outside sources. Reasoning alone, written out with no tools, is chain-of-thought prompting; a fixed plan run by code is a chain.

recall.prompt: A colleague calls their invoice tool an agent. Their code sends each invoice to a model once to pull out the supplier and total, compares the total with the purchase order (the company's record of what it ordered) in code, then posts the result to the ledger (the accounts book), always in that order. Is it an agent? What would make it one, and what would that cost?

keyIdeas.idea: No: the code fixes the order of the steps, so it is a fixed chain, a workflow
An agent lets the model choose its next action each time from what it observed, looping until it is done or a stop condition ends it
The cost: less predictable, harder to test, more calls, so it needs only the tools it needs and limits

recall.model: It isn't an agent. The code fixes the order, extract, compare, post, every time, so it is a fixed chain, a workflow. The model fills in one step but never chooses what happens next. It would become an agent if the model were given tools, say look up the purchase order, query the supplier, post or hold, and chose the next action at each step from what it observed, looping until it decided it was done or a stop condition ended it. That buys flexibility for invoices nobody planned for, at a cost: it is less predictable, harder to test, and takes more calls. If it ever needs that, it gets only the tools it needs, read-only where possible, and a step cap in code. For a job with known steps, the chain is usually the better build.

recall.prompt: Ulla's agent ran with the stop condition "when the model says it is done" and a step cap of 20. Which is true of Tuesday night?
options: The model decided it was finished at 03:20
The step cap in Elvet's code ended the run at step 20; the model never said it was done
The surgery's system ended the run by no longer replying
Taking away send would have ended the run at step 12, just after CANCEL
recall.why: Every reply it sent to the surgery brought back a message asking for another, so with a broad goal the model always had something to answer and never finished. The cap of 20 in Elvet's code ended it at 03:20. Without send, the run ends at step 8 with 5 drafts and nothing sent, and no CANCEL ever leaves.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. Thank you all. Gran's agent has the narrow goal, drafts and never sends, stops at 12 steps, and I read the trace every Sunday. Gran loves her morning list. Then December came. On three nights before Christmas her inbox held 23 emails, 14 of them asking her something: cards, the carol service, the flower guild's wreaths. On each of those mornings there were ten drafts and no list at all. The trace for each of those nights ends at 03:12, at step 12, on a draft_reply, and nothing after it. That week the surgery also wrote about her follow-up appointment, and she didn't see it until the Friday.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did no list come on those three mornings, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The cap ended the run at step 12, two reads and ten drafts, before the finish step that writes the list
Reaching the cap should be reported: your code, not the model, says the run was stopped and lists what was left
Size the cap to the night's mail, or keep a step back for the list

coldCase.model: The cap did its job and nobody heard about it. Steps 1 and 2 read the inbox and the calendar, and steps 3 to 12 drafted replies to the first ten of the 14 questions. At step 12 the cap of 12 ended the run, before the finish step that writes Gran's list, so the surgery's letter, which only the list would have named, sat unmentioned. A cap reached is not a normal ending, and the model can't report it because it isn't running any more. Your code should say so: when the cap stops a run, write a short note for Gran from the trace, the run stopped at step 12, these emails were not looked at, and put it at the top of the list. Then size the cap to the night: a couple of steps per email, worked out from the number in the inbox at 03:00 with a ceiling, or keep a step back so the list is always written. Keep the cap; it is what makes a bad night short.

next: Next, Workflows Before Agents: a factory line that runs itself, and fixed chains of model calls, routing, parallel calls, and when not to use an agent.

sources.title: Shunyu Yao, Jeffrey Zhao, Dian Yu, Nan Du, Izhak Shafran, Karthik Narasimhan, Yuan Cao, ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models, arXiv 2210.03629 (2022), abstract: reasoning traces and task-specific actions in an interleaved manner; reasoning traces help the model induce, track, and update action plans as well as handle exceptions; HotpotQA and Fever with a simple Wikipedia API; ALFWorld and WebShop, absolute success rate of 34% and 10%, with only one or two in-context examples

Anthropic, How tool use works (Claude Platform docs), read 11 October 2026: the model never executes anything on its own; client-executed tools require your application to drive a loop; the canonical shape is a while loop keyed on stop_reason; the loop exits on any other stop reason (end_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence, or refusal); the server-side internal loop has an iteration limit, and a model still iterating at the cap returns stop_reason pause_turn

Anthropic, Tool use with Claude (Claude Platform docs, tool use overview), read 11 October 2026: Claude determines when to call a tool based on the user's request and the tool's description; client tools run in your application; Claude Opus is much more likely to recognize that a parameter is missing and ask for it, and this behavior is not guaranteed

OWASP GenAI Security Project, LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency, OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, read 11 October 2026: damaging actions performed in response to unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated outputs from an LLM; root causes excessive functionality, excessive permissions, excessive autonomy; an extension that accesses a user's mailbox to summarise emails may only require the ability to read emails, so it should not contain other functionality such as deleting or sending messages

ISO/IEC 27001:2022, Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection, Information security management systems, Requirements: Annex A includes control 5.15, access control, control 8.2, privileged access rights, and control 8.15, logging
AICPA, 2017 Trust Services Criteria (With Revised Points of Focus, 2022): the criteria used for SOC 2 reports, including the logical and physical access controls criteria, CC6
